I interpret for boards, so I spend my working life watching people who are competent in one language look uncertain in another, and I want to say something about that. The single most common mistake I see is not a grammar mistake. It is somebody who did not catch the question and answers anyway. They give a long answer to a question nobody asked, and the room quietly decides that this person is not on top of the detail. The fix takes four seconds. Ask them to say it again in a different way. Nobody has ever thought less of somebody for asking that. What they think less of is the answer that misses. And here is the part that surprises people. In my experience, senior visitors expect to repeat themselves. They came a long way, they know their accent is not easy, and they would rather explain twice than be agreed with by somebody who did not follow.

When I visit a site as an investor, I am not looking for a presentation. I have read the numbers on the plane. What I am trying to find out in two days is whether the people running the operation know where the problem is. So my questions are usually small and specific, and they sound harmless. How long does that take. Who signs that off. What happens if the customer does not pay in April. And what I am listening for is whether the answer has a number and a date in it, or whether it has adjectives. If somebody tells me the situation is under control, I have learned nothing. If somebody tells me that four accounts are late, that all four are the same kind of customer, and that they will know more after the harvest, then I trust the whole department, including the parts I did not ask about.
